title: The song of the one who knows
hook: the Taittiriya ends with someone who finds one self in the eater and the eaten, and bursts into song: ha-vu, ha-vu, ha-vu
carry: i am food and eater: one self in all
tomorrow: in the beginning, the self alone

segments.voice: Yesterday: prasad, and the vow, do not despise food. Your line was food is brahman: offer it, share it.
screen: `FOOD IS BRAHMAN: OFFER IT, SHARE IT.`

segments.voice: There's a sound people make when something is too good for words. Not a word, exactly. The noise you make biting into the first ripe mango of the year. The whoop in the car when the song comes on. A baby kicking its feet and shouting at nothing in particular. Scholarly books don't usually end that way. The Taittiriya Upanishad does. Its last lines describe a person who has understood all of it, and that person doesn't give a lecture. They sit down and sing, and the first thing out of their mouth isn't a word at all.
screen: `THE FIRST RIPE MANGO OF THE YEAR.` → `A BOOK THAT ENDS IN SONG.` → `NOT A WORD AT ALL.`

segments.voice: The text says the one who knows moves through these worlds, eating the food they wish, taking the form they wish, and sits singing a chant. It begins: ha-vu, ha-vu, ha-vu. Tradition treats those syllables as stobha: sounds woven into a chant that carry no dictionary meaning. Commentators hear them as a cry of wonder. Then the words come, each line three times. Aham annam. I am food, I am food, I am food. Aham annadah. I am the eater of food, three times. I am the one who makes the verse, three times. Remember yesterday: everything eats and is eaten. This singer has stopped standing outside that chain, judging it. They've found themselves on both sides of it. I'm what's eaten. I'm the eater. I'm also the poet who puts them together. Teachers hear in it the Upanishads' central teaching, sung instead of argued: one self, the atman, in every being. The one who serves and the one who's served aren't strangers. And the song keeps going. I am the firstborn of the cosmic order, older than the gods. Whoever gives me away, protects me. Then the last line: I have overcome the whole world. Light like the sun. So the Upanishad that drew a careful map of the layers ends without a map at all. It ends in a voice, singing. Ha-vu. The Upanishad doesn't explain the joy. It lets you hear it.
screen: `THE ONE WHO KNOWS SITS AND SINGS.` · `HA-VU: A SOUND WITH NO DICTIONARY MEANING.` · `I AM FOOD. I AM THE EATER.` · `ONE SELF IN ALL.` · then, large: `AHAM ANNAM.`

segments.voice: If you're somewhere you can, hum very softly on the out-breath, no tune, and feel it buzz in your chest and lips; if you can't make a sound right now, hum inside, silently. The sound doesn't mean anything, so between hums, rest, and see whether it still feels like something.
Stobha, a sound woven into a chant with no dictionary meaning. The Taittiriya's last lines: a singer who has found themselves as both food and eater, opening with ha-vu, a cry of wonder.
Your line: i am food and eater: one self in all. Tomorrow, back to the beginning, with the self alone. See you then.

howItsDone: In Vedic recitation the Taittiriya's third chapter closes with this chant, ha-vu included, and Sama Veda singers still use stobha syllables like these inside the melodies they learn from their teachers.
